# How to read this document

This document is divided into sections based on specific topics. In each section there is a set of summary main bullet points, a description of the analysis done in that section to support those bullet points, and the output from the analysis done in that section. The main bullet points cover a combination of answering the questions in the empirical paper and the overall questions about how each of the estimators perform under different conditions. The analysis descriptions need to be moved to be under the piece of analysis they describe, but for now I thought it was better to have it all up top.

- Are the standard errors targeting finite versus super population 

Relevant section from the empirical paper:

  We discuss this further in our simulations, but the consequence is that any of our standard error estimators can be viewed   as conservative, if we view the clusters as a finite population, or as appropriate if we consider the clusters as coming     from a larger superpopulation (Litschwartz et al., 2025). 
  
- Do estimated standard errors vary across estimators and why?

Notes:
Is this because true SEs vary across estimators?
Is this estimation error?
Are certain SE estimators more accurate than others?
  
Relevant section from the empirical paper:
Choosing an estimand and excluding the fully interacted estimators results in estimated standards errors that are less variable across estimators. However, it is notable that differences are still often non-trivial. Even in Figure  we see estimated standard errors are 20 percent different across estimators in 24 percent of the cases we examined. 

- Are the fully-interacted models driving the instability of the estimated standard errors?

Relevant section from the empirical paper:

 For example, the largest estimated standard error is 1.5x the smallest estimated standard error in only 10 percent of cases without the fully-interacted models, down from 44 percent when considering all estimators. The ratio never exceeds 1.8 once the fully-interacted models are excluded. This corroborates simulation findings that show the instability of estimated standard errors coming from fully-interacted estimators (Litschwartz et al., 202X). In general, we do not recommend using the fully-interacted estimators due to this short-coming. 

- Are problems caused by low degrees of freedom due to estimate instability or bias?

Relevant section from the empirical paper:
Notice that in Figure 2 it appears that choice of estimator matters more in low-degree of freedom studies – the ranges across estimators tend to be larger in low degree of freedom studies (blue dots) than high degree of freedom studies (red dots).

# Are any of the estimators ever substantially biased? When? 

In 90% of the scenarios we tested for all of the estimators the magnitude of the bias was less than .01 (Figure 1), and the scenarios with bias require the confluence of multiple bias causing factors (Figure 2). For clarity we just present the results from the full factored simulation, but results from the low degrees of freedom results showed the same patterns. The estimators theory says are unbiased do indeed have nearly no bias (or have very low bias) across the full range of simulations. The person weighted fully interacted did estimator had bias as bad as -.033 in the worst 5% of scenarios tested, which from the regression tree requires a correlation between the treatment effect and cluster size and a small number of clusters per block (Figure 2). For the remaining estimators, except the multi-level fully interacted model, the bias was as bad as -.2, which was primarily driven by the combination of dissimilar blocks and unbalanced treatment assignment of the clusters. The fully interacted multi-level model performed fine with dissimilar blocks and unbalanced treatment assignment, and overall only bias as bad as .1. However, all the multi-level models had bias in the simulations where there was a correlation between the number of clusters and the treatment effect, and the cluster-level ICC was zero, and there was large within block variance in cluster size.

## Main Bullet Points:

- 
- All analysis done on the fullfactor simulation, because the results didn't change in the low degrees of freedom simulation

- Methods that are as bad as -.2 in the 5% of scenarios with the most bias: LRapw-FE-db, MLM-RE, MLM−FE, LRa−FE−db

- LRapw−FE−db: In the worst 5% of the sims bias as big as -.2. Fine as long as blocks aren't messy or aren't unbalanced or J.bar is S. If unbalanced but J.Bar is S and also cor_J_tau is not zero, that can be a problem.

- MLM−FE, mostly no bias when blocks aren't messy, except cor_J_tau != 0 & ICC.sch=0 & cv.sch!=0, when blocks are messy than bias is at J.bar M,L and p.bar is unbalanced

- LRa−FE−db: In the worst 5% of the sims bias as big as -.2. As long as the blocks are not messy it's fine. Bias needs combination J.Bar is Large and unbalance, otherwise it's fine.

- MLM−FIcw has bias as bad as .1 in the 5% of scenarios with most bias,  bias is when cor_J_tau != 0 & ICC.sch =0 & cv.sch!=S  
- The LRapw−FIpw−db . This is consistent with theory. 
- LRa−FIcw−db: no bias in any case


- MLM-RE, mostly no bias when blocks aren't messy, except cor_J_tau != 0 & ICC.sch=0 & cv.sch!=0, when blocks are messy than bias is at J.bar M,L and p.bar is unbalanced


- For most of the estimators that are biased, the mean bias is mostly driven by large differences across blocks. With the largest bias in cases with large differences across blocks, 10 or 20 clusters, and unbalanced assignment to treatment (mean p =.7).


## Description of Analysis

- The first graph is a boxplot of mean bias across the different scenarios by method. The faint horizontal lines go out to the full range, the bars are the 1% to 99%, and the boxes are the 10% to 90%.

- The second graph is a regression tree which predicts the magnitude of the mean bias using different data generating parameters and also flags for if the method is an MLM, is fully interacted, is cluster weighted, or is person weighted.

- The third graph is a the same regression tree above, but just for the LRapw−FIpw−db. The indicators for MLM, FI, cluster weighted, and person weighted are dropped for this regression.   

- The first table contains the DGPs that produce that largest magnitude of mean bias for each method, conditional on the magnitude of the mean bias being at least .1 . Where again mean bias is the mean bias against the targeted estimator. 


```{r bias, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE}

sruns.graph.bias<-sruns.clean  %>% filter(method %in% core.methods) 

bias_plot_full <- create_custom_boxplot(
  sruns.graph.bias %>% filter(group == "full_factor"), 
  "bias.s.estimand", 
  "Super Population Mean Bias by Method", 
  "Mean Bias",
  vline_at = 0
)

print(bias_plot_full)

```

```{r biastree, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
# Simple faceted analysis trees
methods <- unique(sruns.graph.bias$method)[!(unique(sruns.graph.bias$method) %in% c("LRa-FIcw-db"))]

   
# Set up plotting layout
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))

for (method_name in methods) {
  create_analysis_tree(
    sruns.graph.bias %>% filter(method == method_name, group == "full_factor"), 
    outcome_var = "bias.s.estimand.mag", 
    predictor_vars = c("block_type", "J.bar", "cor_J_tau", "sd.sch", "ICC.sch", 
                       "cv.sch", "num.cov", "p.bar"),
    tree_title = paste(method_name)
  )
}

# Reset plotting parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


# Are any of the estimators generally more precise than others? When? 
In general all the different estimators have comparable precision (Figure 3). Excluding the multi-level estimators, within a given scenario and a targeted estimand (person weighted vs. cluster weighted) all the estimators have standard errors that are at most 10% larger than the median. The multi-level estimators become more precise when there is the combination is large variation in cluster size and the school ICC is zero, otherwise their precision is close to the other estimators (Figure 4).  


```{r standard errors, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE}

sruns.graph.stab<-sruns.clean  %>% filter(method %in% core.methods) %>% 
                                   mutate( SE.s.norm=(SE.s/SE.s.median),
                                           SE.s.norm.weight=(SE.s/SE.s.median.weight))
stab_plot <- create_custom_boxplot(
 sruns.graph.stab %>% filter(group=="full_factor"), 
  "SE.s.norm.weight", 
  "True Standard Error by Method", 
  "Normalized True Super Population Estimate Standard Error",
 vline_at = 1,
   log_scale = TRUE
)+scale_y_log10(
  limits = c(0.5, 1.5),  # Sets the min and max values shown on the axis
  breaks = c(0.5,.7,.8,.9,1.0,1.1,1.2,1.3,1.5)
)
print(stab_plot)
```
```{r standard errors tree, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE}

tree2<-create_analysis_tree( sruns.graph.stab %>% filter(group=="full_factor"), 
                            outcome_var = "SE.s.norm.weight", 
                             predictor_vars = c("is_MLM", "block_type","J.bar", "cor_J_tau",
                                                "sd.sch", "ICC.sch", "cv.sch", "num.cov", "p.bar"),
                            tree_title = "Decision Tree for Super Population True Standard Error")


```

```{r low df checks, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
lowdf<-sruns.clean %>% filter(group=="lowdf")
with(lowdf,table(is.na(mean.SE.hat)))
na_ids <- lowdf %>% filter(is.na(mean.SE.hat)) %>% pull(ID) %>% unique()


lowdf.complete <- lowdf %>% filter(!(ID %in% na_ids))
lowdf.complete <- lowdf.complete %>% select(all_of(DGP_vars),block_type_lowdf) %>% unique()

lowdf.ncomplete <- lowdf %>% filter((ID %in% na_ids))
lowdf.ncomplete <- lowdf.ncomplete %>% select(all_of(DGP_vars),block_type_lowdf) %>% unique()

with(lowdf,table(J.bar,K))
with(lowdf.complete,table(J.bar,K))
with(lowdf.ncomplete,table(J.bar,K))

#what ran

# none when K was 20
#when J.bar is L and K is 10 than 2 scenarios ran

#only keep the sets where K==7

incomplete_methods <- c("LRa-FIcw-db", "LRa-FIcw-het", "LRapw-FIpw-db",
```

# Which estimators produce the best estimates of the treatment effect standard error?

1) Assess, for each estimator, when the standard errors are systematically too high or too low

o These are all E[SE-hat] / SE, so all comparisons are internal to the estimator.

o Again identify boxplots of ranges, and then identify when an estimator has a long tail to being too low.


2) Assess, for each estimator, when is coverage poor for the estimators?

a. Calculate coverage for each scenario

b. Repeat the above.

```{r infl, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
sruns.graph.infl<-sruns.clean  %>% mutate(perc.off.SE.s=abs((mean.SE.hat-SE.s)/SE.s)*100)

sruns.graph.infl.ff <- sruns.graph.infl %>% filter( group=="full_factor")
sruns.graph.infl.lowdf<-sruns.graph.infl %>% filter( group=="lowdf" & !(method %in% incomplete_methods))

inf_plot <- create_custom_boxplot2(
  sruns.graph.infl.ff, 
  "inflate.s",
```
